title: Who but You
hookLine: who but You would do this, Lord, raising the lowly to honor (Maru, Ravidas, ang 1106)
carry: raise the lowly to the heights
tomorrow: His family carried the dead cattle

cards: Over a king's head, in the old courts of India, an attendant held a canopy. Without a word, it said: this one is honored.

Now hold that canopy over a leather-worker from Benares, a man whose trade made people step aside in the street. That's the picture Ravidas paints in a hymn in Raag Maru, and he can hardly believe it himself.
His question gives today its name.

teach.h: GAREEB NIVAAJ: WHO CHERISHES THE POOR.
teach.b: The hymn sits on Ang 1106 of the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase, it opens: O Beloved, who but You could do such a thing? Then comes a name for God worth learning: gareeb nivaaj, the one who cherishes the poor.

teach.h: THE CANOPY ON A LEATHER-WORKER'S HEAD.
teach.b: My Lord, Ravidas sings, places the canopy over my forehead. The royal sign, on him. He doesn't soften what he was in other people's eyes.
His touch, he says, was counted as polluting the world, and on that very person the Lord has poured mercy.

teach.h: THE LOWLY RAISED, AND NO FEAR.
teach.b: Then the line at the hymn's heart: You raise the lowly to the heights, my Gobind, and You fear no one. That last part is quiet but sharp.

Lifting someone a whole town has agreed to keep low takes nerve, and Ravidas's Lord doesn't flinch. Then the hymn opens a door. Ravidas names others carried across the same way: Namdev, Kabir, Trilochan, Sadhna and Sain.
Namdev, the cloth-printer whose milk was drunk and whose temple turned, filled this past week; Kabir came earlier in this block; Trilochan, Sadhna and Sain are still ahead on this path.

Ravidas lines them up like witnesses: it wasn't only me. The hymn closes, in paraphrase: says Ravidas, listen, holy people, the Lord does everything. So the title is a question that isn't really a question.
Who but You is what someone says when they've been lifted, and know they didn't lift themselves.

how: Ravidas's hymns are sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, with the same respect given to the Gurus' own hymns, and this one is often sung as a song of thanks for being raised up.

o: a royal canopy held over a king's head
a poor man who lives on the gifts of others
the one who cherishes the poor, a name for God

games.q: inside the hymn — tap the pairs.
p: the one who cherishes the poor
the king's sign, over Ravidas's head
raises the lowly and fears no one

s: Ravidas hides what people thought of his birth
he says it plainly: his touch was counted as polluting, and mercy came to him anyway.
the hymn names other devotees besides Ravidas
Namdev, Kabir, Trilochan, Sadhna and Sain.
the hymn ends with Ravidas praising his own effort
it ends: listen, holy people, the Lord does everything.

games.q: you're Ravidas, and the Lord has held a royal canopy over your head. who do you say did it?
o: I earned it by my devotion.
the town finally changed its mind.
games.why: the hymn ends: says Ravidas, listen, holy people, the Lord does everything. even the list of saints is a list of others the Lord carried.

practice: Let faces come: someone overlooked at work, a relative people talk past, a neighbor nobody greets, a kid at the edge of the room.

Stay with one, and picture a small canopy over them: their name said in front of others, their opinion asked first, a thank-you where it can be heard. If you pray, let Waheguru go with each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Gareeb nivaaj. The one who cherishes the poor: Ravidas's name for the Lord who held a king's canopy over a leather-worker's head.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the cherisher of the poor, Ravidas's name for the Lord in this hymn (Ang 1106).

carryVoice: Your line: raise the lowly to the heights. The week ran from everything is Gobind, to Namdev's sultan, to Ravidas's city without sorrow. Day seven hundred seventy-seven, done.
